title: ICU care bundles and infection prevention
summary: ICU care bundles and infection prevention: the daily FAST HUGS BID checklist, VAP, CLABSI and CAUTI prevention bundles, VTE and stress ulcer prophylaxis, hand hygiene and isolation precautions, and pressure injury prevention with early mobilisation.

topics.title: Daily ICU checklist (FAST HUGS BID)
topics.summary: A structured daily review that catches the routine preventive items most often missed.

definition.text: FAST HUGS (Vincent 2005) is a mnemonic for daily ICU review: Feeding, Analgesia, Sedation, Thromboprophylaxis, Head-of-bed elevation, Ulcer (stress ulcer) prophylaxis, Glycaemic control. 'BID' is a widely used extension: Bowel care, Indwelling catheter removal, De-escalation of antimicrobials.

steps.title: Feeding
steps.detail: Is the patient fed? Enteral nutrition within 48 h unless contraindicated; review target and tolerance.

steps.title: Analgesia and sedation
steps.detail: Analgesia first; target light sedation (RASS 0 to -1) unless a specific indication for deep sedation; daily sedation interruption paired with SBT.

steps.title: Thromboprophylaxis
steps.detail: Pharmacological prophylaxis unless contraindicated; mechanical (IPC) if bleeding risk; reassess daily.

steps.title: Head of bed
steps.detail: Elevate 30-45° in ventilated patients unless contraindicated (spinal injury, haemodynamic instability).

steps.title: Ulcer prophylaxis
steps.detail: PPI/H2RA only in high-risk patients (ventilated, coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease); stop when the risk resolves.

steps.title: Glucose
steps.detail: Insulin when glucose ≥ 180 mg/dL; target 144-180 mg/dL; avoid hypoglycaemia.

steps.title: Bowel care
steps.detail: Bowels opened? Laxative protocol for patients on opioids; check for diarrhoea (C. difficile testing when indicated).

steps.title: Indwelling devices
steps.detail: Is each central line, arterial line, urinary catheter and drain still needed? Remove if not.

steps.title: De-escalation
steps.detail: Review cultures and antimicrobial need daily; narrow, stop or set a duration.

tables.title: FAST HUGS BID checklist
rows: At RASS target? Can sedation stop?

tables.caption: Use at the morning round and document each item.

redFlags.text: A missed thromboprophylaxis dose for > 24 h in an immobile ventilated patient - restart or document why it is held.

pitfalls.text: Ticking the checklist without acting on it - assign each item to a named person.
Continuing stress ulcer prophylaxis indefinitely after extubation or transfer.

pearls.text: Pair the spontaneous awakening trial with the spontaneous breathing trial each morning - both reduce ventilator days.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Most ICU complications (VTE, VAP, CLABSI, GI bleeding, pressure injury, oversedation) are preventable with simple measures that are easily forgotten during acute management. Checklists convert these into reliable daily habits.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- FAST HUG concept [Vincent 2005].
- PADIS guidance on light sedation [Devlin 2018]; SHEA 2022 VAP prevention essentials [Klompas 2022].
- REVISE 2024 for SUP in ventilated patients [Cook 2024].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Which items deserve a mandatory daily check versus clinician judgement; glucose targets in specific groups.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Use the checklist as a printed or electronic form at the bedside; in high-load Indian ICUs a nurse-led checklist read aloud at rounds improves compliance.
- The NCDC 2020 IPC guidelines recommend bundle compliance audits for HAI prevention.

topics.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle
topics.summary: Essential VAP/VAE prevention practices from SHEA 2022: avoid intubation, minimise sedation, SAT/SBT, mobility, head-up, subglottic drainage and oral care.

definition.text: VAP: pneumonia developing > 48 h after intubation. SHEA 2022 classifies prevention practices as essential (good evidence, low risk) and additional; the focus has shifted to reducing ventilator days and ventilator-associated events (VAE).

steps.title: Avoid intubation
steps.detail: Use HFNC or NIV where appropriate to prevent intubation.

steps.title: Minimise sedation
steps.detail: Avoid benzodiazepines; target light sedation; daily spontaneous awakening trials.

steps.title: Daily SBT
steps.detail: Paired with SAT, to extubate at the earliest opportunity.

steps.title: Early mobility
steps.detail: Progressive rehabilitation as tolerated.

steps.title: Subglottic drainage
steps.detail: Use endotracheal tubes with subglottic secretion drainage for patients expected to need ventilation > 48-72 h.

steps.title: Head of bed
steps.detail: Elevate 30-45°.

steps.title: Oral care
steps.detail: Toothbrushing (without chlorhexidine) at least twice daily.

steps.title: Circuit care
steps.detail: Change ventilator circuits only if visibly soiled or malfunctioning; keep cuff pressure 20-30 cmH₂O.

tables.title: SHEA 2022 VAP prevention (adults)
rows: Avoid intubation (HFNC/NIV); minimise sedation; SAT + SBT daily; early mobility; subglottic drainage tubes if > 48-72 h; head-of-bed 30-45°; change circuits only when soiled
Selective oral or digestive decontamination (in settings with low antimicrobial resistance); daily toothbrushing
Chlorhexidine oral care; probiotics; silver-coated tubes; routine stress ulcer prophylaxis for VAP prevention; early tracheostomy for VAP prevention
tables.caption: Summary of SHEA/IDSA/APIC 2022 recommendations; see source for full grading.

redFlags.text: New fever, purulent secretions, rising FiO₂/PEEP after ≥ 2 days of stable ventilation: suspect VAP or other VAE - culture and assess (see icu-infections module).

pitfalls.text: Chlorhexidine 0.12% oral rinse as routine VAP prevention - not recommended, possible harm.
Leaving the bed flat during transfers, imaging and procedures.

pearls.text: The strongest VAP prevention is a shorter ventilation episode: every bundle element that shortens ventilation counts.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Microaspiration of colonised oropharyngeal and gastric secretions past the endotracheal cuff, biofilm on the tube and impaired cough/mucociliary clearance cause VAP. Sedation and supine positioning increase aspiration.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- SHEA/IDSA/APIC 2022 compendium update [Klompas 2022].
- PADIS guidance on sedation minimisation [Devlin 2018].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Selective digestive decontamination in high-resistance settings such as India; VAP definitions and surveillance using VAE.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Device-associated infection rates in Indian ICUs are higher than in high-income countries, with a large share caused by carbapenem-resistant Gram-negatives - bundle compliance audits are central (NCDC 2020).
- Subglottic drainage tubes cost more and may not be stocked; prioritise them for patients expected to be ventilated beyond 72 h.
- Selective digestive decontamination is not recommended in high-resistance settings.

topics.title: CLABSI and CAUTI prevention
topics.summary: Insertion and maintenance bundles for central lines and urinary catheters, and nurse-driven removal.

definition.text: CLABSI: laboratory-confirmed bloodstream infection in a patient with a central line in place > 2 days without another source. CAUTI: UTI in a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter > 2 days. Both are largely preventable with insertion and maintenance bundles.

steps.title: Line insertion checklist
steps.detail: Hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full-body drape), observer with authority to stop the procedure.

steps.title: Skin antisepsis
steps.detail: Alcoholic chlorhexidine (> 0.5% CHG in alcohol); allow to dry.

steps.title: Site and guidance
steps.detail: Ultrasound guidance; avoid the femoral site in obese adults when another site is suitable; subclavian has the lowest infection risk.

steps.title: Maintenance
steps.detail: Scrub the hub before every access; CHG-impregnated dressings; change transparent dressings every 7 days (gauze every 2 days) or when soiled/loose; daily CHG bathing in ICU patients.

steps.title: Remove
steps.detail: Daily review of line necessity; remove unnecessary lines promptly; replace lines inserted in emergencies without full asepsis within 48 h.

steps.title: Urinary catheter indication
steps.detail: Insert only for appropriate indications (acute retention, accurate output monitoring in critically ill, perioperative, sacral wounds in incontinent patients, end-of-life comfort).

steps.title: Urinary catheter care
steps.detail: Aseptic insertion; closed drainage system; bag below bladder level and off the floor; unobstructed flow.

steps.title: Urinary catheter removal
steps.detail: Daily review; nurse-driven removal protocols; consider external catheters or intermittent catheterisation; do not screen or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

tables.title: Central line bundle checklist
rows: Hand hygiene; maximal sterile barrier; alcoholic CHG; ultrasound guidance; best site; checklist with observer
Hub disinfection; CHG dressing; dressing change schedule; daily CHG bath; dedicated PN lumen
Is the line needed? Remove if not

redFlags.text: Fever with pus or erythema at the insertion site, or septic shock with a line in place: take paired blood cultures (line and peripheral) and remove the line.

pitfalls.text: Sending urine cultures from catheterised patients without symptoms, then treating asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Keeping a central line only for blood sampling convenience.

pearls.text: Routine scheduled replacement of central lines or guidewire exchange does not reduce CLABSI.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Early CLABSI (< 7 days) is mainly extraluminal from skin flora tracking along the catheter; later infection is mainly intraluminal from hub contamination. CAUTI arises from extraluminal biofilm ascent or intraluminal reflux; risk rises about 3-7% per catheter day.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- SHEA 2022 CLABSI compendium [Buetti 2022].
- SHEA 2022 CAUTI compendium [Patel 2023].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Antimicrobial-impregnated catheters and lock solutions as routine; CHG bathing in low-incidence units.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- CHG-alcohol skin prep and CHG dressings are available but cost is a barrier; prioritise insertion asepsis, hub scrubbing and early removal, which cost little.
- NCDC 2020 guidelines describe device bundles and HAI surveillance for Indian facilities.

topics.title: VTE and stress ulcer prophylaxis
topics.summary: Choosing pharmacological or mechanical thromboprophylaxis, renal and obesity dosing, and who needs stress ulcer prophylaxis after REVISE.

definition.text: Critically ill patients are at high VTE risk. ASH 2018 recommends pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH preferred over UFH) over none, and mechanical prophylaxis when anticoagulants are contraindicated. Stress-related mucosal bleeding risk is highest in ventilated patients and those with coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease.

steps.title: Assess bleeding risk
steps.detail: Active bleeding, platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L, recent neurosurgery/intracranial haemorrhage, severe coagulopathy, planned neuraxial procedure.

steps.title: No contraindication
steps.detail: LMWH: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (dalteparin 5,000 units daily is an alternative). CrCl < 30 mL/min: enoxaparin 30 mg daily or UFH 5,000 units SC every 8-12 h.

steps.title: Contraindication
steps.detail: Intermittent pneumatic compression; start pharmacological prophylaxis as soon as bleeding risk allows. Adding IPC to pharmacological prophylaxis gives no extra benefit (PREVENT).

steps.title: Special cases
steps.detail: Obesity: higher doses (see drug); trauma, burns, spinal cord injury: earlier and more intensive prophylaxis per trauma guidelines; HIT: non-heparin anticoagulant.

steps.title: SUP: who
steps.detail: Invasive mechanical ventilation, coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease (high risk). Not routinely for low-risk patients.

steps.title: SUP: what
steps.detail: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV/enteral daily (or H2RA); REVISE showed fewer clinically important UGI bleeds in ventilated patients with no mortality difference.

steps.title: Stop
steps.detail: Stop SUP when the risk factor resolves (extubation, shock resolved); do not continue at discharge.

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg, CrCl 80 mL/min: enoxaparin 40 mg SC at 18:00 daily. If CrCl falls to 25 mL/min: 30 mg daily or switch to UFH 5,000 units SC every 12 h.
doseCards.notes: Range: 30 mg daily (CrCl < 30) to 40 mg every 12 h (BMI ≥ 40).
doseCards.verify: Renal and obesity dose adjustments per local protocol.

doseCards.role: VTE prophylaxis in severe renal impairment

doseCards.workedExample: Ventilated 70 kg patient: pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily; stop after extubation if no other indication.

tables.title: Stress ulcer prophylaxis decision
rows: Invasive ventilation; coagulopathy (platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L, INR > 1.5); shock; chronic liver disease
Recent peptic ulcer, Barrett's, dual antiplatelets with GI risk
tables.caption: Based on the 2021 clinical practice guideline and REVISE 2024.

redFlags.text: Unilateral leg swelling, unexplained tachycardia or hypoxaemia despite prophylaxis: evaluate for DVT/PE.
Platelet fall > 50% from day 5-10 of heparin: assess for HIT (4T score) and stop all heparin if likely.

pitfalls.text: Holding LMWH for days 'in case of procedures' without a plan to restart.
Graduated compression stockings alone in ICU - IPC is preferred when mechanical prophylaxis is needed.

pearls.text: Give the evening dose of LMWH at a fixed time so that morning procedures can be timed 12 h after the dose.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Immobility, venous injury from lines, inflammation and hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad) drive ICU VTE. Stress ulceration results from splanchnic hypoperfusion, mucosal ischaemia and impaired bicarbonate secretion; acid suppression reduces bleeding but may increase pneumonia and C. difficile.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ASH 2018 guideline: LMWH preferred; pharmacological over mechanical [Schünemann 2018].
- PREVENT (2,003 patients): adjunctive IPC did not reduce proximal DVT [Arabi 2019].
- SUP-ICU (3,298): pantoprazole did not change 90-day mortality [Krag 2018].
- REVISE (4,821 ventilated patients): pantoprazole reduced clinically important UGI bleeding (1.0% vs 3.5%) without mortality difference [Cook 2024].
- 2021 SUP guideline: suggest SUP in high-risk patients only [Ye 2021].
consultantNotes.controversies: - SUP in the sickest patients (SUP-ICU subgroup signal of harm in high severity, not confirmed by REVISE); anti-Xa guided dosing in obesity and renal failure.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Enoxaparin biosimilars are widely available and affordable; IPC devices are limited in many ICUs - prioritise them for patients with contraindications.
- Stress ulcer prophylaxis is often over-prescribed on general wards in India and continued at discharge; use the ICU daily checklist to stop it.

topics.title: Hand hygiene, standard and transmission-based precautions
topics.summary: WHO 5 moments, choosing contact, droplet or airborne precautions, and MDRO cohorting.

definition.text: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent healthcare-associated infection. Standard precautions apply to every patient; transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) are added for specific organisms.

steps.title: WHO 5 moments
steps.detail: Before touching a patient; before a clean/aseptic procedure; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; after touching patient surroundings.

steps.title: Method
steps.detail: Alcohol-based hand rub 20-30 s for most situations; soap and water 40-60 s when hands are visibly soiled and for C. difficile or norovirus.

steps.title: Standard precautions
steps.detail: Hand hygiene, PPE for anticipated exposure, respiratory hygiene, safe sharps, cleaning of equipment and environment, safe waste and linen handling.

steps.title: Contact
steps.detail: Gloves and gown on entry; dedicated equipment; single room or cohort: MDR Gram-negatives (CRE, CRAB), MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, scabies.

steps.title: Droplet
steps.detail: Surgical mask within 1-2 m; single room or cohort: influenza, meningococcal disease (first 24 h of effective therapy), pertussis, diphtheria.

steps.title: Airborne
steps.detail: N95 respirator (fit-tested), airborne infection isolation room (negative pressure, ≥ 12 air changes/h where available): pulmonary/laryngeal TB, measles, varicella and disseminated zoster.

steps.title: Aerosol-generating procedures
steps.detail: Intubation, NIV, bronchoscopy, open suctioning in patients with respiratory pathogens: N95, eye protection, gown and gloves.

steps.title: Audit and feedback
steps.detail: Direct observation audits (WHO tool), surveillance of HAIs and MDROs, feedback to staff.

tables.title: Transmission-based precautions
rows: CRE, CRAB, MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, scabies
Gown + gloves; single room or cohort; dedicated equipment
Surgical mask; single room or cohort; ≥ 1 m spacing
Pulmonary TB, measles, varicella, disseminated zoster

redFlags.text: Cluster of the same MDR organism in 2 or more patients: notify the infection control team for outbreak investigation.

pitfalls.text: Gloves used as a substitute for hand hygiene, or the same gloves worn between patients.
Alcohol rub for C. difficile - it does not kill spores; wash with soap and water.

pearls.text: Most hand hygiene failures occur at moments 4 and 5 (after patient or surroundings contact) - put alcohol rub at every bed space.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Healthcare workers' hands are the main vehicle of cross-transmission; the patient environment (bed rails, monitors, ventilator surfaces) is a reservoir for MDR Gram-negatives and C. difficile spores.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- WHO 2009 hand hygiene guideline and 5 moments [WHO 2009].
- CDC/HICPAC isolation precautions [Siegel 2007].
- NCDC national IPC guidelines for Indian healthcare facilities [NCDC 2020].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Contact precautions for endemic MRSA/VRE versus universal gloving; cohorting where single rooms are scarce.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Single rooms and negative-pressure rooms are scarce in Indian ICUs; NCDC 2020 supports cohorting of patients with the same organism, dedicated staff where possible and ≥ 1 m spacing between beds.
- High CRE/CRAB prevalence makes environmental cleaning and hand hygiene compliance the main control levers.
- Airborne precautions for TB are frequently needed given the high national TB burden.

topics.title: Pressure injury prevention and early mobilisation
topics.summary: Risk assessment, repositioning, support surfaces, device-related injuries, staging, and how hard to mobilise after TEAM.

definition.text: Pressure injury: localised damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence or under a medical device, from pressure or pressure with shear. ICU patients are at high risk because of immobility, sedation, vasopressors, oedema and devices.

steps.title: Assess risk
steps.detail: On admission and daily with a structured tool (Braden ≤ 18 indicates risk) plus clinical judgement; inspect skin including under devices.

steps.title: Reposition
steps.detail: Individualised repositioning schedule (commonly 2-4 hourly), 30° lateral tilt; avoid positioning on existing injury or erythema.

steps.title: Support surface
steps.detail: High-specification reactive foam or active (alternating pressure) mattress for at-risk patients.

steps.title: Heels and sacrum
steps.detail: Offload heels (heel elevation devices or pillows under calves); consider prophylactic multilayer silicone foam dressings on sacrum and heels.

steps.title: Devices
steps.detail: Check and pad under NG/ET tubes, NIV masks, oxygen tubing, collars and catheters; reposition devices regularly.

steps.title: Prone patients
steps.detail: Protect face, chest, knees and other pressure points; reposition head every 2 h.

steps.title: Skin and nutrition
steps.detail: Manage moisture and incontinence; optimise nutrition and protein.

steps.title: Mobilise
steps.detail: Daily assessment for rehabilitation: in-bed exercises progressing to sitting, standing and walking when stable. Avoid aggressive maximal early mobilisation in the first days of ventilation (TEAM).

tables.title: Pressure injury staging (NPIAP/EPUAP)
rows: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis
Full-thickness skin loss; fat visible; no bone, tendon or muscle
Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, muscle or cartilage
Persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration

redFlags.text: Deep tissue injury (purple, boggy skin) over the sacrum or heels in a patient on vasopressors - it may evolve to stage 3-4 within days; offload immediately.

pitfalls.text: Massaging reddened skin over bony prominences - not recommended.
Forgetting device-related injuries from ET tube ties and NIV masks.

pearls.text: TEAM showed that maximising early active mobilisation did not increase days alive out of hospital and caused more adverse events - mobilise steadily as part of usual care rather than maximally.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Sustained pressure above capillary closing pressure and shear cause tissue ischaemia; deep muscle is more vulnerable than skin, so injury may start deep and appear later. Vasopressors, hypotension and oedema reduce tissue tolerance. Immobility drives ICU-acquired weakness.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- International EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA guideline 2019 [EPUAP 2019].
- PADIS 2018: rehabilitation/mobilisation suggested [Devlin 2018].
- TEAM (750 ventilated patients): increased early active mobilisation did not improve days alive out of hospital and had more adverse events [TEAM 2022].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Optimal repositioning intervals on modern mattresses; the right dose and timing of rehabilitation.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Alternating pressure mattresses may be limited; regular manual repositioning and heel offloading are low-cost essentials.
- Family members often help with repositioning and physiotherapy in Indian ICUs - train them with clear safety rules.
- Pressure injury incidence is a nursing quality indicator under NABH accreditation.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.indications: VTE prophylaxis in critically ill adults
drugs.adultDose: Prophylaxis: 40 mg SC once daily. CrCl < 30 mL/min: 30 mg SC once daily (or use UFH). BMI ≥ 40: 40 mg SC every 12 h is commonly used.
drugs.renalHepatic: Accumulates in renal failure - reduce dose or switch to UFH; consider anti-Xa level (prophylactic target 0.2-0.5 units/mL).
drugs.cautions: Hold 12 h before neuraxial procedures/LP and before most surgery; avoid in active bleeding, platelets < 30-50 × 10⁹/L, HIT.
drugs.verify: Obesity dose (40 mg every 12 h vs weight-based 0.5 mg/kg daily) per local protocol.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (subcutaneous)
drugs.indications: VTE prophylaxis, especially in severe renal impairment or when rapid reversal may be needed
drugs.adultDose: 5,000 units SC every 8-12 h (every 8 h in higher-risk or obese patients).
drugs.monitoring: Platelet count every 2-3 days from day 4 to day 14 of exposure.

drugs.name: Pantoprazole
drugs.indications: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients
drugs.adultDose: 40 mg IV (or enteral) once daily; stop when risk factors resolve.
drugs.preparationIndia: 40 mg vial for IV; 40 mg tablets (cannot be crushed - use IV or a suitable liquid alternative via tube).
drugs.cautions: Possible association with C. difficile infection and pneumonia; avoid continuing at ICU or hospital discharge without an indication.

drugs.name: Famotidine
drugs.cautions: Delirium/confusion in elderly and renal impairment; thrombocytopenia (rare).
drugs.verify: IV famotidine availability in India (oral tablets widely available).
